content:
For a while, I've been trying to work out the best way for me to talk about HR and the Employment Rights Act in written form. 


It didn't feel right to include it on my business websites, because it's not really part of my business. 

So I have done a thing. And bought a domain which is literally just my name. 

It feels like a thing that's very unlike me. 

But it means I can share my actual thoughts with the world! 

And I hope it might lead to more opinion and comments in the press about HR and the absolute  💩  we have to put up with people saying about us. 

My first article is titled "The Real Problem with HR Isn't HR" - and it serves as a reminder to some that HR could be the difference between a criminal charge and a massive fine. 

Read it here: https://lnkd.in/gJMMBmWk

content:
Prevention of (sexual) harassment guidance is changing again next month. 


"Reasonable steps" to prevent it is now "all reasonable steps". 

I don't actually see the difference, but what do I know. 

And employers have to take steps to prevent third-parties from harassing employees. Note: this is not just sexual harassment, it is all forms of harassment. 

I once told a room full of pub managers about this and they all literally laughed at me. Anyway... 

Again, all of my prevention of sexual harassment risk assessments already featured third-parties. Because my risk assessments were based on the existing ECHR guidance. 

Anyway, if you're as confused about all of this as I am, my latest article on this topic from The HR Vault can be found here: https://lnkd.in/gPYd9ZJb 

You can download updated harassment policies and risk assessments from the Vault now too!

content:
Another new claim for employees to bring…


…another claim that doesn’t stand alone. 

Like the requirement for the statement of particulars, prevention of sexual harassment and a variety of others I can’t be bothered to recall, this one will not stand alone. 

In English, this means that it can’t be the only thing brought to the tribunal. Another claim, such as unfair dismissal, has to be successful first. 

This one is telling employees about their right to join a trade union. 

🙄🙄🙄 

I think it’s pretty obvious to anyone that knows me: I’m not a fan of what the government are doing to employers. 

I hate this sort of legislation, because it’s not actually benefiting anyone in my opinion. Everyone knows about trade unions. 

And it’s not actually really enforced, is it? 

Sure, the chances of a claim being brought against an employer are higher than ever. We have a smaller workforce and a flooded Tribunal system, therefore, more chance. 

But they are still small. 

And some lawyers have some aggressive tactics to force/frighten claimants into settling (🤮). 

Most claims drop off before they hit the courtroom. 

So employers don’t really have much motivation to bother with these things. 

And don’t really care. 

But, HR colleagues, I’m about you. We will be in trouble if we don’t advise about this! 

You can find an article about the guidance we have to date on The HR Vault here: https://lnkd.in/gxkAay4P

Spoiler alert: there’s about six weeks until this legislation goes live and there’s no final guidance yet. 

Oh wait, that’s not a spoiler! This is always what happens!

content:
The government has published its response to the flexible working consultation 🎉 


It confirms the process you will have to follow before turning down a request, once the regulations land in autumn 2027.

Right now you can refuse a flexible working request on one of eight statutory grounds, having consulted the employee first. That's it.

From autumn 2027, refusing on one of those grounds won't be enough. You'll also have to show the refusal was reasonable, and explain in writing why.

You will have to hold a meeting before rejecting a request.

Not a box ticking exercise either. The government added a line after the consultation making clear the meeting has to be held with a view to reaching agreement. 

So no five minute call with the decision already made and a diary invite for cover.

The meeting sits inside the existing two month window for deciding a request. You give fair notice of it and say why you are calling it. No fixed notice period. 

The government looked at one week and rejected it.

Afterwards you confirm the outcome and the decision in writing. A summary, not minutes.

What you do not get: 
 🚀 requirement for the actual decision maker to be in the room
 🚀 statutory right of appeal
 🚀 statutory right to be accompanied (although non-statutory guidance will keep encouraging the last one. 'Encouraging' is doing a lot of the work in that sentence.)

Acas consults on an updated Code next, due before Parliament by early summer 2027, with guidance on the reasonableness test itself promised later this year.

But the good news is... it's dead easy to just agree to a flexible working request! So... yay! 

Put this on next year's list. Right underneath everything else already on it  😭 

Full legal update from The HR Vault here: https://lnkd.in/gJQqGWZi
